title: Logical Operators
description: Combining conditions with and, or and not, and why Java stops reading early.

content.real: A ride sign: "12 or older AND 1.40 m tall"
content.text: Real conditions have several parts. Logical operators join booleans into one answer.

items.sub: true only when both sides are true
true when at least one side is true

content.caption: `age >= 12 && height >= 1.40` also works in one line, but named parts are kinder to the reader. Use two characters: a single `&` or `|` means something else.

items.title: && (and)
items.code:
true  && true   // true
true  && false  // false
false && false  // false
items.text: Only true when **both** sides are true.

items.title: || (or)
items.code:
true  || true   // true
true  || false  // true
false || false  // false
items.text: Only false when **both** sides are false. Read it as "at least one": `true || true` is `true`.

content.question: What does `System.out.println(false || true);` print?
content.explain: `||` needs just one true side, and the right side is true.

content.value: `!` goes in front of a boolean and flips it. Use it when the question you have is the opposite of the one you want.

content.caption: The last two ask the same thing. Prefer the plain `score < 50`; save `!` for named booleans like `!gameOver`.

content.value: Mixed together, `!` goes first, then `&&`, then `||`. Rather than remember that, use brackets or build the condition in named steps.

steps.note: `day == 6` is true, so the `||` is true.

content.title: Building a condition in named steps
content.outro: `day == 6 || day == 7 || onHoliday` would work too, but three names tell a reader what each part means.

content.value: Maths allows `1 <= n <= 10`, Java does not. A range needs two comparisons joined by `&&`: `n >= 1 && n <= 10`.
content.title: Ranges

content.question: Which line checks that `n` is from 1 to 10?
content.explain: Two full comparisons joined by `&&`. With `||` every number would pass, since each is either at least 1 or at most 10.

content.value: With `&&`, a false left side means the answer is false, so Java skips the right side. With `||`, a true left side is enough. This is **short-circuit evaluation**.

steps.label: people > 0
steps.detail: Checked first. Suppose it is false

content.title: A guard on the left
content.caption: So a safety check on the left can protect something risky on the right.
Sample run: type `0` then `900` and it prints `Affordable each: false` instead of crashing. Swap the two sides and it would crash: order matters.
Putting it all together. Sample run: `80` and `70` gives true, false, false, false. Next module, `if` turns each boolean into a fork in the road.

practice.question: Ask for a number and print whether it is between 1 and 10, using two comparisons joined with `&&`.
Store a day number (1 to 7) and print whether it is a weekend, using `||`. Then print whether it is a weekday, using `!`.
Predict each line before running. Four of these print true and four print false.

quiz.question: When is `a && b` true?
options: Only when both a and b are true
When at least one of them is true
quiz.explain: `&&` means and: every part has to be true. One false anywhere makes the whole thing false.

quiz.question: What does `false || true` give?
options: true, because || needs only one true side
false, because the first side is false
quiz.explain: `||` means at least one. It is false only when both sides are false.

quiz.question: How do you test that an `int n` is between 1 and 10 inclusive?
quiz.explain: Java cannot chain comparisons the way mathematics does, so a range is two comparisons joined with `&&`. Using `||` there would be true for almost every number.

quiz.question: `boolean gameOver = false;` What does `!gameOver` give?
quiz.explain: `!` flips the value, so `!false` is `true`. It reads nicely with a well named boolean: `!gameOver` means still playing.

quiz.question: Why does `people > 0 && bill / people <= 500` not crash when people is 0?
options: The left side is false, so Java never evaluates the division.
Java replaces a division by zero with 0.
quiz.explain: This is short-circuit evaluation: once the left side of `&&` is false the answer is settled, so the right side is skipped. Putting the guard first is the whole point.

quiz.question: Which order are logical operators applied in when brackets are left out?
quiz.explain: That is the order, but relying on it makes code hard to read. Add brackets and nobody has to remember.
